question: to the Commission Branko Grims (PPE) Subject:

Legal experts have long been pointing out the controversial nature of early voting in Slovenia’s National Assembly elections. Article 69 of the Slovenian Elections Act (ZVDZ) clearly states: ‘Voting shall take place at a special polling station within the district election committee’s area.’ In clear violation of this, however, in Ljubljana, for example, as many as 14 districts vote at a single location, namely Stožice. This means that voters in at least 13 districts are in violation of the law, as they are required to vote outside their district. For voters living far away, this process can be an obstacle, which effectively violates their right to participate and the constitutional principle of equality. In total, there are as many as 26 such illegal districts in Slovenia. Further doubts about the fairness of the election are raised by the coalition’s persistent refusal to release the results of early voting as they come in. Instead of counting ballots daily, recording the results and signing the minutes, ballots are kept uncounted for several days in boxes that are unsealed. They are not counted until Sunday. Security for the ballot boxes in Ljubljana is provided by Mayor Zoran Janković’s office, which, given his political prominence, raises legitimate doubts about the neutrality of the process. Can the Commission therefore answer the following question: Does it intend to address electoral procedures, such as rules governing early voting, in its future reports on the rule of law in Slovenia?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.6.2026) As enshrined in Articles 2 and 10 of the Treaty on European Union, democracy is a founding value on which the EU is built. Free and fair elections are at the core of democracy. The Commission does not have a general power to intervene in electoral matters of the Member States. The conduct and the organisation of elections are the competence and responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their national constitutional and legislative rules, while respecting their international obligations and EU law. National competent authorities and courts have the primary responsibility of ensuring compliance with these rules. Electoral procedure is not specifically included in the scope of the annual Rule of Law Report. The Commission supports Member States’ efforts to ensure free and fair elections, particularly through the European Cooperation Network on Elections1, and relying on its Recommendation on inclusive and resilient electoral processes in the Union2. To address the growing and evolving challenges to democracies across the EU, the Commission adopted the European Democracy Shield in November 20253. In this context, among other initiatives, the Commission will develop a repository of common references and standards for electoral processes, based primarily on exchanges within the European Cooperation Network on Elections.
